title: New 'Blue Zone' of Long-Lived People Found in Sardinia
paragraphs: The Italian island of Sardinia is already famous as one of the world's "Blue Zones," places where people live unusually long lives. Now, researchers say they may have found a new one on the same island.

The new candidate is Bolotana, a small mountain village in central Sardinia, about 110 kilometers from the original Sardinian Blue Zone. The study was published in the journal Frontiers in Aging by researchers from the University of Sassari in Sardinia, working with partners in the US, including Dan Buettner, who made the idea of Blue Zones famous.

The researchers carefully checked official records, comparing them with church records of baptisms and burials to make sure people's ages were correct. They found that among 3,060 people born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925, 38 lived to be 100 or older. This means the village had 1,242 people who reached 100 for every 100,000 births, compared with 793 for Italy as a whole.

Interestingly, the village's long life was mainly seen among women. For women aged 70, the expected remaining life was 20.85 years, compared with 18.06 years for Italy. The chance of a 70-year-old woman reaching 100 was 13.83%, more than three times the Italian average. For men, the advantage was much smaller. This is different from the original Sardinian Blue Zone, where men and women live long lives in similar numbers.

However, the researchers say Bolotana is a "promising candidate," not yet an official Blue Zone. Because the village is small, with only around 2,300 people, the results are uncertain. The results also changed depending on the years studied.

The researchers could not explain why people in Bolotana live so long. They also noted that the long lives of people in other famous Blue Zones, such as Okinawa in Japan, may have become less unusual in recent years. They say more studies are needed to understand the roles of genes, lifestyle, social connections and health care.
